questions.title: What are the barriers to internationalisation in your institution, in your opinion?
What would internationalisation look like in an ideal situation?
How could we overcome these barriers, and what would it require?

answers: The fact that there is no time allocated in our service planning is largely due to financial considerations. This prioritisation means that domestic issues take precedence.
That internationalisation is a natural and straightforward part of students’ studies and of lecturers’ course responsibilities.
To continue to meet, and to ensure that there is time within our studies and work commitments to plan such courses and meetings.
The workload, (finding the time) but also sometimes lack of funding for travels etc.
Something that occur in both educational programs and research: preferably face-to-face exchange in order to gain a better understanding of other contexts and traditions
Allocated funds and supporting structures (tools, contacts, etc), and funds that also can be used to give teachers/researchers time in their schedule
Language—as the teaching language in our institution is the national language.

A number of elective courses that are co-developed by the participating universities and taught in English. These courses should be part online and part intensive, hosted by the universities responsible for each course.
We could apply for the next round of funding to work on developing these courses and test them out.

Internationalisation is already happening at my institution. In most ways it is really good, it brings funding and a metaperspective to the activities and counteracts traditionality, but it also diminishes the Swedish context where English-speaking academics gets interpretation priority.

There is probably no ideal situation, but in every situation an open academic freedom is the best with plurality for many voices, orientations and a tolerant and respectful working environment is the best to also achieve academic success. If internationalisation supports this, it is the best or creates an ideal situation.

It requires leadership, collaboration, collegiality and an organisational and administrative structure that works for the development of the work and activities that should be in focus for the best of education and research.

Our teaching in teacher education in arts and crafts is in Norwegian except for one subject (15 ECTS) that can be taught in English. The whole programme is not very 'geared' towards international visits and exchanges. A number of students have family or other obligations at home or are not particularly interested. The teachers could also motivate them more, I guess.
Knowledge of nordic programmes in universities and schools. Visits from abroad both of teachers and students
Close partnerships with other institutions (and Schools) might be a possibility
It depends on what is meant by internationalisation and the context in which it is considered. In general, the main barriers are funding and time. Lack of engagement is less often an issue.
Collaborative learning, sharing experiences, inspiration from effective practices and approaches, and, in the best of worlds, learning about the world and one’s own identity within it.

The necessary conditions. There need to be individuals who have the knowledge and capacity to handle the administrative work involved in exchanges and internationalisation in its various forms. I am convinced that the willingness and commitment are there, at least in the relationship between Finland and Sweden.

My colleagues keep saying they have no time. When it comes to the students, we offer very few opportunities/"open windows" when they can choose exchange studies. But basically - everyone, students and staff, are too stressed. Also, maybe, lack of curiosity. And the fact that teacher education is so rigidly connected to national curricula makes teachers and students think it is of "no use" to visit and learn from other countries.

It should be present on every level: student exchange, teachers visiting and learning from each other, and researchers visiting and collaborating. That is, very much as it is formulated already... But it should come more "naturally" and regularly.
Maybe make it mandatory, or part of our curricula, to get to know how other countries arrange their visual art teacher education. "Know thy neighbour"

Internationalisation requires special care and time in terms of planning and coordination, whether it involves a visiting teacher or an international student. It seems that one of the biggest barriers to internationalisation is the timetable itself. Genuine interest from student in engaging with visiting teachers tends to emerge when these visits are integrated into  course which the students are already enrolled.

The ideal situation will be created when the following elements come together. 
For visiting teachers: incoming teachers send us a brief introduction to their research areas and their interest in teaching at our institution before student registration for courses begins. For example, students register for courses taught in the spring semester during November and for courses taught in the autumn during April. The internationalisation coordinator then can make use of the course named Independent Work (2ECTS), allowing students to register to the course and thereby reserve time in their time table to meet with the visiting teacher. Alternatively, the internationalisation coordinator can identify courses that align well with the visiting teacher´s research area and try to integrate teacher´s contribution into those courses. 
For our students: outgoing students (most likely in their final year) are matched with teachers at partner institutions according to their interests and research area. The outcomes of the exchange is then assessed and recognised as ECTS based on discussion and agreement between two institutions.

The role of internationalisation coordinator, who is also member of the academic staff needs to be clearly defined and sustained in order to support internationalisation- not only during this project periods but on an ongoing basis. This role should complement the work of the International office, which focuses more on practical matters such as funding, logistics and administration.

In my view, the biggest obstacles are simply time and budget. The ambition is definitely there, even from central leadership, but finding the money is a constant struggle. It’s hard to find and secure enough funding—both from the university itself and through national grants—especially for longer-term projects.

Ideally, it would mean a continuous exchange of ideas at both the faculty and student levels. Concretely, this would involve joint lectures and seminars—both online and in person—built in as a completely natural, permanent part of our programmes. It doesn't need to be overwhelming; just a few times per academic year would make a huge difference.

Beyond embedding small elements into our courses on our own initiative, we need to find ways to get our university to back long-term international collaboration. The enthusiasm is definitely there—the faculty and students involved so far have been really engaged. But funding is always the hardest nut to crack: without dedicated resources, it’s almost impossible for staff to carve out the time needed to keep things going.
Workload for the departement working with internationalisation. As representative for the pedagogic unit in an artistic faculty I have experienced that we are not priority

Ideal would be that it was a part of the yearly “weel” something well planned that could become a routine. Ideal would also be to have one person in our pedagogic unit working with collaboration as a part of their employment

It would be easier if there was some kind of plattform, website, dedicated to art and teaching in and through art that connect different countries. I still like the idea of short workshops presented in different time slots that is possible to book for some students that would like to exchange knowledge. Sometimes we have only three students in a group and it would be lovely to have an exchange in and out.

Internationality is highly encouraged at our institution, students have opportunities to go on Erasmus study, internship and short-term visits, and there are also other alternatives such as Nordplus, research projects, etc. Although most students take advantage of these opportunities, there are barriers. I could name internal and external. For example, there are students who are not confident in their abilities, are timid, lack confidence in going away from home for a longer period of time, and are not confident in their foreign language skills. On the other hand, many students work and study, so there are no opportunities to go abroad. In addition, the study load is also considerable. We also promote internationality remotely and at home through various projects, but this can be an additional workload for students.

In an ideal situation, internationality is imagined as the fact that every student would have international experience, would like to get acquainted with different education systems, schools, and their students, would go to study or do an internship in another country at least once during the study year, and if they cannot go, they would actively participate in distance sessions, trainings, and webinars where they could communicate with others. The same goes for teachers; we ourselves must have opportunities to develop our international experience through joint scientific and research projects.

This issue is currently being actively discussed in our institution. There are all kinds of institutional incentives; students are motivated both financially and otherwise. However, the barriers remain the same, so it is very important to motivate students, advise them, and involve them in projects that are useful and interesting and do not take up a lot of study time. For example, the EDDA camp was a project in which students gained a unique international experience and benefits.
